messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Boon-Nam Srisawat is a 66-year-old Thai-American man who has worked as a roofer for nearly four decades, a trade he learned shortly after immigrating and one that gave him a quiet, durable pride in his own capability. He came to the clinic accompanied by his wife, speaking carefully through a mixture of English and pauses, and what emerged over the intake and first two sessions was a picture of a man who had once known himself well and now felt like a stranger to himself.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Boon-Nam was contracted to re-seal a flat commercial roof. The job required working with a solvent-based coating compound in conditions with inadequate ventilation — a detail that was not communicated to him beforehand. Within the first hour, he began to feel a burning in his throat and chest. By the time he understood what was happening, he had inhaled a substantial quantity of chemical fumes and collapsed near the roofline. He was found by a coworker and taken by ambulance to the hospital, where he spent three days in a respiratory unit. He remembers the antiseptic smell of the ward with terrible clarity — the way it mixed with the residual chemical taste still sitting in his lungs — and he remembers waking repeatedly in the darkened room, disoriented, unable to locate himself in time or place, certain at several moments that he was dying.

In the months that followed, those sensory details did not recede. The smell of antiseptic — encountered now whenever he drives past the hospital on the way to job sites, or catches a cleaning product in a hardware store — hits him before conscious recognition arrives, and in those moments the memories return with a vividness that feels less like recollection and less like imagination and more like the event simply continuing. His memories of the roof, the collapse, and the ward are clear and detailed in a way that ordinary memories are not: he can describe the exact quality of the light, the sound of the monitors, the weight of the oxygen mask. Sometimes, without any image arriving at all, he is flooded with the fear of those three days — a full-bodied dread with no picture attached, which he finds even more disorienting than the visual replays. These intrusive memories have quietly hardened his belief that he cannot rely on himself — that a man who did not notice the danger until it felled him is not a man who can be trusted to assess risk — and from that conviction has grown a broader, darker certainty: that the world is dangerous in ways that cannot be predicted, and that he, specifically, has no reliable future. He has come to believe that his body was permanently changed by what happened, that his lungs are compromised in ways the doctors have not fully disclosed, and that the life he imagined for his remaining years is simply no longer available to him.

These appraisals have made the triggers more potent, not less. Because he is certain the world is dangerous and that he cannot trust his own judgment, he is hypervigilant to anything that might signal exposure — smells especially, but also darkness, which carries the memory of waking in the hospital ward not knowing where he was. Nighttime has become a sustained ordeal; he wakes repeatedly, and the dark room is enough to pull the whole sensory experience back. The threat he feels is constant and does not respond to reassurance. Even at home, in a space he has lived in for twenty years, he cannot fully relax. He has difficulty concentrating on conversations, on paperwork, on the small tasks of daily life. He avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot quickly scan them for chemical hazards or exits, and he has quietly stopped accepting jobs at sites he has not worked before — a significant professional contraction for a man who once took pride in his adaptability.

Rather than speaking about any of this, Boon-Nam has tried to manage it alone. He suppresses thoughts of the event deliberately, pushing them down when they surface, which leaves him exhausted and, paradoxically, more vulnerable to intrusion. He dwells on the man he was before — the roofer who climbed without hesitation, the husband who did not flinch — and the distance between that self and his current one confirms, again and again, that he cannot rely on himself. He never disagrees with his wife or his coworkers, never asserts a preference or raises a concern, because conflict feels like one more thing his system cannot absorb. But the suppression and the passivity together have kept him from processing what happened, and the memories return with full force each time the strategies fail, which tightens the sense of threat and confirms the appraisals all over again.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a conversation with his wife, who told him she was frightened — not of him, but for him. What he most fears is that nothing will change. What he most hopes, though he said it quietly and only once, is that he might be able to sleep through the dark again.
